notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Exodus 2, drawn from the sources accessed.

---

**v. 1:** The "man of the house of Levi" is Amram, and the "daughter of Levi" is Jochebed, identified in Exodus 6:20. The phrase "there went" (Hebrew idiom) indicates this marriage had occurred some time before — Amram and Jochebed had already had Miriam (about age 14–15 at this point) and Aaron (about 3 years old). The edict of Pharaoh demanding the death of male infants was likely issued between Aaron's birth and Moses'. Marrying within the same tribe was proper to keep the tribes distinct. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/2.htm) | [Pulpit (via excerpt)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/2.htm) | [Garner-Howes Baptist](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-2.html) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm)

**v. 2:** Jochebed saw that Moses was a "goodly" (beautiful, well-formed) child. Ellicott notes that Stephen calls Moses "comely before God" (Acts 7:20). The Hebrew writer makes clear this hiding was an act of faith — "by faith Moses… was hidden three months by his parents, because they saw he was a beautiful child; and they were not afraid of the king's command" (Heb 11:23). The parents trusted God's promise to deliver Israel. [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-2-commentary) | [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/2.htm) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm)

**v. 3:** The "ark" (Hebrew *tebah*) is the same word used for Noah's ark — the only two places it occurs in Scripture. This links Moses' deliverance to Noah's. The "bulrushes" are papyrus, an Egyptian plant growing 10–15 feet tall. "Slime" is bitumen/mineral pitch imported from Mesopotamia and used for embalming; "pitch" is vegetable pitch. Jochebed technically obeyed Pharaoh's command — she put her son in the river — but did so in a way that preserved his life. She placed it among the reeds (*suph*) so the current wouldn't carry the basket away. [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm) | [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-2-commentary) | [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/2.htm)

**v. 4:** "His sister" is Miriam. She was probably placed there by her mother to observe. Calvin comments that the parents had "some hope remaining, though it was but small" — Miriam was set to watch "rather to witness her brother's murder, than to provide for the safety of the child." Yet God's secret providence brought Pharaoh's daughter to the river. [Calvin](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/exodus-2.html) | [Pulpit (via excerpt)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/2.htm) | [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/2.htm)

**v. 5:** Pharaoh's daughter came to bathe. Ellicott notes this was consistent with Egyptian customs — the Nile was considered sacred and its waters health-giving; royal women had reserved bathing places. The princess was accompanied by her maidens (*na'aroth*). Josephus calls her Thermuthis; other sources give her various names. Jewish tradition says she had recently lost a child. [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm) | [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/2.htm) | [Garner-Howes Baptist](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-2.html)

**v. 6:** The princess opened the basket herself. The baby wept — and her compassion was stirred. Guzik says "in God's guidance… she was conditioned by her culture and upbringing to reject the Hebrews, but the cry of baby Moses melted her heart." She immediately recognized him as "one of the Hebrews' children" — likely from the circumstances (no Egyptian mother would need to expose her child) or, as Jewish commentators add, from his circumcision. [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/2.htm) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm)

**v. 7:** Miriam's prompt offer shows her quickness and intelligence. The Talmud and Josephus record a tradition that the princess tried Egyptian wet-nurses but the baby refused them all — giving Miriam the perfect opening. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/2.htm) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm)

**v. 8:** Jochebed must have been waiting nearby, ready to appear. Ellicott comments that she was "eagerly expecting — perhaps, while concealed from sight, watching the result." [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm)

**v. 9:** Jochebed became her own child's paid nurse. Guzik notes this as God rewarding the faith of Moses' mother — she trusted God by hiding Moses and then by setting him on the river, and God gave him back to her with wages. Gill notes a Jewish tradition that she was paid two pieces of silver a day. [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/2.htm)

**v. 10:** The child grew and was brought to Pharaoh's daughter, probably at weaning (about age 2–3). He "became her son" — whether by formal adoption (though Ellicott notes we have no evidence adoption was an Egyptian custom) or by being raised as a son. The name "Moses" comes from the Hebrew *mashah* ("to draw out"). The princess used a Hebrew etymology, suggesting she understood Hebrew (or Jochebed explained it). In Egyptian, "Mesu" meant "born" or "son" and appears in names like Ra-mesu (Ramesses). Moses thus received both Egypt's finest education (Acts 7:22 — "learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians") and formative Hebrew nurture from his own mother. Guzik notes Josephus' claim that Moses was heir to the throne and led Egyptian armies against the Ethiopians. No doubt "it was in these early years that Moses learnt of the 'God of the fathers'" (Cole). [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm) | [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/2.htm) | [Bible.org](https://bible.org/seriespage/preservation-and-preparation-israel%E2%80%99s-deliverer-exodus-2)

**v. 11:** Acts 7:23 tells us Moses was "full forty years old" at this point. The phrase "looked on their burdens" means more than seeing — Cole notes it means "to see with emotion… with distress." Hebrews 11:24–26 explains what was happening in Moses' heart: by faith he "refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God." Moses deliberately identified with the Hebrews. [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm) | [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-2.html)

**v. 12:** Moses "looked this way and that way" — the actions of a man who knew he was about to do wrong. He killed the Egyptian and buried him in the sand. Ellicott says the act was "clearly the deed of a hasty and undisciplined spirit. The offence did not deserve death." Acts 7:25 explains his motivation: "he supposed that his brethren would have understood that God would deliver them by his hand, but they did not understand." Moses was trying to do God's work in man's wisdom and strength. Constable (Dallas Theological) comments: "Moses' desire to help his brethren was admirable, but his methods were deplorable… He trusted in his own ability." The NET note (cited at Precept Austin) calls this "trying to do God's work by the flesh." [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm) | [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-2.html) | [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-2-commentary)

**v. 13:** The next day Moses tried to mediate a dispute between two Hebrews. Ellicott says he acted "as any man of position and education naturally interferes to stop a quarrel," without offensive assumption of authority. [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm) | [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/)

**v. 14:** The Hebrew's retort — "Who made you a prince and a judge over us?" — exposed Moses' fatal error. His previous day's killing had stripped him of moral authority. The question prefigures Israel's later rejection of Moses (and ultimately points toward Christ, who was also rejected as prince and judge). Moses feared — not the fear of the Exodus departure (Heb 11:27), but the immediate fear that his crime was known. [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm) | [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/2.htm)

**v. 15:** Pharaoh sought to kill Moses — a just response under Egyptian law, where murder was a capital crime. Moses fled to Midian, southeast of Egypt (in the Sinai peninsula or present-day Saudi Arabia). Guzik notes Moses probably felt "that God's plan for his life was completely defeated" — but "at this point, Moses was right where God wanted him." [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm) | [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-2.html)

**v. 16:** The "priest of Midian" had seven daughters. Midianites were descendants of Abraham through Keturah (Gen 25:1–2), so they likely worshipped the true God. Reuel's name means "friend of God." Drawing water and tending flocks was normal work for daughters of a chief in that culture. [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm) | [Bridgeway](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-2.html)

**v. 17:** The shepherds drove the women away — apparently a habitual bullying (see v. 18). Moses "stood up and helped them." Here, unlike in Egypt, Moses' intervention was legitimate defense, not murder. In Egypt he had been served; in Midian he became a servant. Ellicott says Moses "has learnt wisdom by the past, and uses no unnecessary violence." [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm)

**vv. 18–19:** Reuel (also called Jethro) noticed his daughters returned early. They described their rescuer as "an Egyptian" — based on his dress and appearance, since Moses still wore Egyptian clothing (Kaiser). [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm)

**v. 20:** Reuel's rebuke to his daughters reflects Bedouin/Arab hospitality — it was offensive to leave a stranger without inviting him to eat. [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm) | [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/)

**v. 21:** Moses "was content to dwell with the man." He married Zipporah (meaning "warbler" or "little bird," Cole). Guzik observes: "In Egypt Moses learned how to be somebody. In Midian he learned how to be nobody." Trapp said, "Much he had learned in Egypt, but more in Midian." [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm)

**v. 22:** Gershom means "a stranger there" (from *ger* = stranger, *sham* = there). The name expressed Moses' loneliness — he belonged neither among the Egyptians nor the Hebrews. Guzik warns against thinking these were merely "waiting" years: they were hard working years that shaped Moses for his calling. [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm)

**v. 23:** "After a long time" (literally "in those many days") — about forty years (Acts 7:30). The king of Egypt died. If the Exodus occurred ~1446 BC, the Pharaoh from whom Moses fled reigned over forty years (possibly Thutmose III or Rameses II). The Israelites "groaned" — they had perhaps hoped a new king would ease their burdens, but he did not. Their cry "came up unto God." [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm) | [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-2.html)

**vv. 24–25:** God "heard," "remembered His covenant," "saw," and "took notice" (or "acknowledged" / "was concerned about them"). This fourfold response is pivotal. "Remembered" does not imply God had forgotten; it means He turned His active attention toward them. God's response was based on His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — not on Israel's merit. Constable notes this is "another of the many references in Scripture that indicate that prayer affects some of God's actions." The miraculous action beginning in Exodus 3 is the result of these cries. [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/2.htm) | [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-2.html) | [Bible.org](https://bible.org/seriespage/preservation-and-preparation-israel%E2%80%99s-deliverer-exodus-2)

---

## Denominational Distinctives

**Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin emphasizes God's secret providence throughout the chapter. He insists that "all things which led to the preservation of Moses, were disposed by his guidance… to ascribe to fortune such an harmonious combination of various and manifold means, is no less absurd than to imagine with Epicurus that the world was created by the fortuitous conjunction of atoms." God "drew out Moses, who was to be the future redeemer of his people, as from the grave, in order that he might prove that the beginning of the safety of his Church was like a creation out of nothing." [Calvin](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/exodus-2.html)

**Baptist (Spurgeon, cited at Precept Austin):** Spurgeon stresses that the parents' hiding of Moses was "by faith" — not mere natural instinct. Faith "is sanctified common sense… It is not fanaticism; it is not absurdity. It is making God the grandest asset in our account, and then reckoning according to the soundest logic." On the believer's security, he draws a parallel: "Even though Moses was brought to the place of death, he was secure in the ark. The word 'ark' is the same word for Noah's ark. It is a picture of Christ." [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-2-commentary) | [Garner-Howes Baptist](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-2.html)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word – David Guzik):** Guzik emphasizes application for the believer's spiritual life. Moses had to be "broken of his self-reliance and royal pretensions" — "he was too big for God to use." The chapter teaches that "God's plans often work in ways that contradict our own logic and require us to surrender our own strength." The parallel between Moses and Jesus is developed: both were "favored by God from birth… offered deliverance to Israel… rejected with spite." [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/)

**Dispensational (Constable – Dallas Theological):** Constable sees Moses' failure as a lesson that "he must not trust in his own ability but rely on God's strategy and strength." Prayer is highlighted as genuinely affecting God's actions: "This is another of the many references in Scripture that indicate that prayer affects some of God's actions." [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-2.html)

---

## Other Views

**Catholic/Orthodox:** The searches to newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org did not return usable content within the search limit. However, Guzik notes that Origen (an early Christian writer from Alexandria) allegorized this passage extensively: Pharaoh represents the devil; the male and female children represent the rational and animal aspects of the soul; the two midwives are the Old and New Testaments; Pharaoh's daughter represents the church; the waters of the Nile represent baptism; the law (Moses) is taken into the church and grows to spiritual maturity. Guzik quotes Clarke's caution that in this kind of allegory, "every passage and fact might then be obliged to say something, any thing, every thing, or nothing, according to the fancy, peculiar creed, or caprice of the interpreter." [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/)

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes, cited at Precept Austin):** The NET note characterizes Moses' killing of the Egyptian as "trying to do God's work by the flesh" and divides the chapter into two parts: the failed attempt to deliver (vv. 11–15) and Moses' introduction to life as deliverer in Midian (vv. 16–22). It frames the chapter as an "interesting study in the presumption of the leader." [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-2-commentary)

**Jewish Tradition (noted in multiple commentaries):** Josephus claims Moses was heir to Egypt's throne and led victorious armies against the Ethiopians. Jewish legends say his birth was painless, his face illuminated the room like the sun and moon, and he walked and spoke at one day old. The Talmud records that Pharaoh's daughter tried Egyptian wet-nurses but the baby refused them all (because he was destined to speak with God). [Guzik/Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-2/) | [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/2.htm)
